problem: Imitation learning from shortest-path planners was believed to generalize poorly (e.g. 4.4% ObjectNav on MP3D in prior work), while RL is slow and needs reward shaping, and human demonstrations are too expensive to scale.
motivation: Simulators can cheaply generate unlimited privileged-planner trajectories if house diversity is sufficient. The authors observe that with ~200k procedural houses, strong pretrained visual encoders and long-context transformers, plain behavior cloning of shortest-path experts yields agents that explore, backtrack and transfer to the real world with RGB only.
key_idea: Behavior-clone shortest-path planners at massive scale and diversity (~200k ProcTHOR/Objaverse houses) with an end-to-end goal-conditioned transformer (SigLIP features, 100-frame context) using RGB only, so it transfers zero-shot to a real Stretch robot.
insight: Diversity of houses, not exploratory experts, is what makes shortest-path IL work: 10k houses x10 episodes beats 100 houses x1000 episodes by 13.5 SR points, and an exploration-based expert gives no gain (46.5 vs 57.0 SR). Encoder and context matter: SigLIP nearly doubles CLIP-RN50's average SR (49.9 vs 26.6) and window 10/50/100 gives 27.8/39.9/49.9. Failures are mostly perception: GT detection lifts ObjectNav from 55.0 to 85.0.
method: Goal encoder: pretrained SigLIP (or T5) text encoder produces token embeddings of the instruction.

Goal-conditioned visual encoder: SigLIP patch features from navigation and manipulation RGB cameras, MLP-projected, with camera-type embeddings, concatenated with goal tokens and a CLS token, passed through a 3-layer transformer encoder to give a per-step visual vector.

Action decoder: 3-layer causal transformer decoder over past visual vectors plus previous-action embeddings, sinusoidal time encodings and an object-in-hand sensor, cross-attending to the goal; predicts 1 of 20 discrete actions; cross-entropy teacher forcing. Trains with a 100-step window and random time-index shifts (up to 900) so it can use full history at inference.
Procedural data: ~200k ProcTHOR houses (191,568 sampled) with 41,133 Objaverse+THOR assets, WordNet-annotated; ~90k episodes per task.
Expert planners: navmesh shortest-path navigation, iterative-distance-minimization pick-up, DFS room-center visitation, all using privileged simulator ground truth.
Augmentation: color jitter, blur, random crop, posterization and sharpness, applied at both train and test time to bridge sim-to-real gap.
Optional detection variant: bounding-box coordinates (GT in sim, DETIC in real) encoded and fed to the visual encoder; real-world grasping uses a heuristic DETIC+FastSAM grasp planner.

setting.backbone: SigLIP-ViT-B/16 image+text encoders (pretrained) + 3-layer transformer encoder and decoder trained from scratch, d=512
setting.model_size: not stated (3-layer encoder/decoder, 512-d, 8 heads, on frozen-size SigLIP-B/16 features)
setting.training_data: Shortest-path expert trajectories in ~200k procedural houses (ProcTHOR + Objaverse); ~90k episodes per task, e.g. 99K ObjectNav episodes / 5M frames; no human demos, no RL
setting.observation: Two RGB cameras (navigation + manipulation) 224x384, plus binary object-in-hand sensor; no depth, no GPS
setting.action_space: 20 discrete actions: base move ±20 cm, rotate ±6°/±30°, arm x/z ±2/±10 cm, wrist rotate ±10°, pickup, dropoff, subtask done, terminate
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT detection only in the 'w/ GT Det' variant; experts use privileged info only for training data generation)

results: Multi-task SPOC reaches 49.9% average SR on CHORES-S-15 in unseen houses, beating a SigLIP-upgraded RL baseline (EmbSigLIP, 31.2%) by ~19 points and getting non-zero Fetch where RL gets 0.0; with GT detection it reaches 65.0% (ObjectNav 85.0%). In the real world, RGB-only gets 39.5% average and 56.1% with DETIC.
limitations: Heavily relies on a hand-designed off-the-shelf heuristic grasp planner in the real world; manipulation is not fully end-to-end
Perception is the main bottleneck (GT detection gives +15 to +24.5 SR points); open-vocabulary description tasks are weakest (~30%)
Hardware speed/dexterity limits; Fetch fails to pick up 29% of the time when nearby; real-world evaluation is small (88 trials)
